chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: (Revision K incorporates a complete reprinting of Parts III and IV of the EDD; pages revised are identified with a "Rev. K" notation in the lower-right corner of each page.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The flight program which is structured modularly, is composed of two basic subsystems: the control subsystem and the application subsystem. The control subsystem controls the sequence and order of execution of all programmed functions in the application subsystem.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The application subsystem provides a master pool of all defined LVDC functions which can be used to generate a total flight program configuration for any given mission task. It is composed of a collection of relatively independent, closed program modules. Each application module is designed to perform one or a number of related functions; e.g., accelerometer readings, chi computations, orbital navigation. As new requirements are defined, new modules may be added to the application subsystem. The operational linkage, sequence, and execution of the application modules for a given mission are governed by the Control Program.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The control subsystem consists of the Control Program and a common communications area which allows for centralization of inter-module communications, common data and indicators, and mission or vehicle dependent parameters. The Control Program, composed of sub-programs and tables, controls the execution of application modules, services interrupts and routes control to the appropriate application module on a priority basis, and provides utility operations.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: At flight program assembly time, the application modules and their mode of operation, sequence, and time frame of execution are specified via system macros. The LVDC Assembler automatically selects the specified modules from the application subsystem and appropriately links them to the Control Program and the common communications area. As requirements are changed and new modules are defined, the flight program configuration may easily be changed at assembly time by identifying different or additional modules.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Hence, the modular construction and control concepts of the program provide a high degree of flexibility and ease of maintenance in order to minimize overall impact and response time for modifications due to varying mission requirements.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Control Program is a group of interacting sub-programs whose primary purpose is to control the sequencing and scheduling of the execution of individual application program modules to meet the operational requirements of a given LVDC mission. It examines interrupts and priority control tables to determine order of module execution and provides a means of transferring operational control to and from the modules. The design and organization of the Control Program is based on the use of sets of master queue/control tables by which the application requirements of any given mission can be specified.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The flight program task is divided into distinct mission segments or phases according to different overall vehicle modes of operation throughout the mission. A phase includes all functions required to be accomplished within a certain time frame of the mission such as powered flight or orbital operation. The number of phases and functions within a phase are defined via system macros independent of the Control Program. Functions within a mission phase must be executed at different frequency rates with different timing precisions. Thus, modules, according to their particular timing requirements, are assigned via system macros to operate under a specific sub-program of the Control Program. The structure (see Fig. 1-1) of the Control Program consists of the following sub-programs:

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
• ● Mission Executive: Governs phase-to-phase transition throughout the entire mission.
  • ● Phase Initializer: Initializes master queue/control tables to proper status at the start of each defined mission phase.

The diagram illustrates the control program structure, divided into three main sections: Mission - Phase Initialize, Basic Iterative Cycle, and Interrupt Processing.

  • MISSION - PHASE INITIALIZE:
    • Start of Mission (Oval) leads to Mission Initialize (Rectangle).
    • Mission Initialize leads to T1 Scheduler Schedules First T1 Module (Rectangle).
    • A decision diamond asks "Any more Active Phases?".
      • If "No", it leads to a "Terminal Loop" (Oval).

      • APPLICA-TION MODULE (Hexagon).

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
• ● Non-Interrupt Sequencer: Controls the execution of those modules which make up the basic iterative computation cycle of any phase, i.e., those functions of a non-priority nature which are to be operated as a part of a repetitive, ordered sequence.
  • ● Periodic Processor: Controls the execution of those modules of a non-priority nature but which are to be executed a given number of times within a specified, but not precisely rigid, time frame.
  • ● Interrupt Processor: Services both hardware and program controlled interrupts and routes control to the appropriate program module on a priority basis.
  • ● Timer 1 Scheduler: Schedules the use of the Timer 1 interrupt to control the execution of priority modules which require operation at an exact time or at a precisely cyclic rate.
  • ● Timer 2 Scheduler: Schedules the use of the Timer 2 interrupt to control the execution of priority modules of a lower order than those under Timer 1 but which also require operation at a specific time or rate as precisely as possible.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Mission Executive performs general system initialization, determines which phases of the specified mission are to be executed, selects required control words for phase initialization, gives control to the Phase Initiator to initiate phase execution, and performs all required system terminal housekeeping at mission end. The Phase Initiator sets the module queue status for the selected phase, executes the phase initialization module, and schedules the next Timer 2 operation before passing control to the Non-Interrupt Sequencer.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Upon initial entry, the Mission Executive (see Fig. 1-2) inhibits all interrupts, initiates real time clock readings and initializes accumulated time

    InhibitAll --> ResetINTC[Reset INTC & all Ints. but TLC]
    ResetINTC --> ReadRTC[Read Real Time Clock]
    ReadRTC --> InitInterrupt[Initialize Interrupt Proc. and Enable TLC]
    InitInterrupt --> InitTimer1[Initialize Timer 1 Scheduler]
    InitTimer1 --> InitPhaseTable[Initialize Phase Selection Table Pointers]

    Fig17 --> Timer1[Timer 1 Scheduler]

    PhaseEnd([Phase End Entry]) --> HaltT2[Halt T2 Int. Counter]

The flowchart illustrates the Mission Executive process. It begins with 'Entry from Preflight', followed by a sequence of initialization steps: 'Inhibit all Interrupts', 'Reset INTC & all Ints. but TLC', 'Read Real Time Clock', 'Initialize Interrupt Proc. and Enable TLC', 'Initialize Timer 1 Scheduler', and 'Initialize Phase Selection Table Pointers'. A box labeled 'Figure 1-7' leads to 'Timer 1 Scheduler', which then joins the main loop. The main loop starts with 'Halt T2 Int. Counter' (triggered by 'Phase End Entry') and 'Resequence to Phase Specified' (triggered by 'Phase Rese-ence Entry'). A decision diamond 'All Phases Completed' leads to 'Inhibit all Interrupts Except TLC' and 'Terminal Loop' if 'Yes', or to 'Determine Next Phase' if 'No'. 'Determine Next Phase' leads to another decision diamond 'Next Phase Active'. If 'No', it loops back to 'Halt T2 Int. Counter'. If 'Yes', it proceeds to 'Update Time', 'Select Phase Initialize Module', and 'Set up Control Words for Phase Initializer', finally leading to 'Exit to Phase Init.'.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: in mission and time base reference. The program then performs all initialization required for the proper operation of the Interrupt Processor and the Timer 1 Scheduler.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Timer 1 Scheduler is called to initiate operation of the Timer 1 interrupt counter. Control is then returned to the Mission Executive for phase selection. The Timer 1 interrupt inhibit is not removed until the completion of first phase initialization.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Mission Executive determines the next phase to be executed by means of a special active phase indicator word. This indicator consists of individual bits arranged in chronological order for each phase defined. Each bit indicates whether or not the corresponding phase is to be executed. At program generation time, all phases defined are set active. If there are no more active phases to be executed, the Mission Executive will perform all required terminal housekeeping functions and enter a terminal loop. If any active phases remain to be executed, the next in order is selected. Control words associated with the phase that is to be executed are obtained from the Phase Selection Table and supplied to the Phase Initializer. The Mission Executive then gives control to the Phase Initializer and is not re-entered again until phase execution is completed. Since phase termination will normally be dependent upon a particular function or calculation performed by some application module, it will be the responsibility of that application module to accomplish Mission Executive re-entry at phase end.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Two entry points are provided to terminate a phase. One entry point allows a specific phase to be selected whereas the other entry automatically selects the next chronological phase. Upon phase end entry, the Mission Executive halts the Timer 2 interrupt counter to avoid any Timer 2 interrupt scheduled but not completed in the previous phase. Timer 1 interrupts are allowed to operate during next phase selection and initialization. The program then proceeds to select the next phase or to enter the terminal loop.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Upon entry from the Mission Executive, the Phase Initializer (Fig. 1-3) uses control information supplied to it to set the master queue tables to the initial queue status specified for the selected phase. The information also provides the linkage to the appropriate application initialize module and to the Sequential Control Table for that phase. After all queue tables are initialized, the Phase Initializer executes the user application initialize module which returns control upon completion. The Timer 2 Scheduler is then called to initiate operation of the Timer 2 interrupt counter. At completion of Timer 2 scheduling, control is passed to the Non-Interrupt Sequencer to control the execution of the application modules which comprise the basic iterative cycle.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The basic iterative cycle consists of the Non-Interrupt Sequencer and Periodic Processor sub-programs, both of which are essentially executable tables. These sub-programs control the sequence and time of execution for the majority of the application modules.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Non-Interrupt Sequencer determines if a module under its control is to be executed, and if so, accesses the module and the Periodic Processor. The Periodic Processor determines for modules under its control whether they are to be executed, and if so, if it is time for their execution. When the Non-Interrupt Sequencer has examined each module under its control, it recycles to the first module and repeats the process; hence, the name Basic Iterative Cycle. The iterative cycle, or computation cycle, is terminated when some application module returns control to the Mission Executive at phase end.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Non-Interrupt Sequencer and Periodic Processor determine whether a module is to be executed by means of its queue status. The system queue tables specify for each application module whether the module is queued-in or queued-out. A module which is queued-in will be executed at the proper time. A module which is queued-out will not be executed until it is

chunks.content:
graph TD; Entry([Entry]) --> Init1[Initialize Non-Interrupt Sequencer Table]; Init1 --> Init2[Initialize Periodic Processor Table]; Init2 --> Init3[Initialize Timer 2 Table]; Init3 --> AppModule{{APPLICATION MODULE}}; AppModule --> Figure1[Figure 1-8
Timer 2 Scheduler]; Figure1 --> Exit([Exit to Non-Int. Seq.]);

The flowchart illustrates the Phase Initializer process. It begins with an 'Entry' point, followed by three sequential initialization steps: 'Initialize Non-Interrupt Sequencer Table', 'Initialize Periodic Processor Table', and 'Initialize Timer 2 Table'. These steps lead to the 'APPLICATION MODULE', which then triggers 'Figure 1-8 Timer 2 Scheduler'. The process concludes with an 'Exit to Non-Int. Seq.' point.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: queued-in. Changing a module's executable status is known as queuing. System macros are provided so that a module at any time may change its own or another module's queue status.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Essentially, the Non-Interrupt Sequencer (Fig. 1-4) consists of a number of tables: a Sequential Control Table for each phase of the mission and a single Sequential Queue Table for the total mission. Each control table is an executable table; i.e., it is made up of executable instructions. It is actually one of these tables that is given control at completion of phase initialization. The selected table will remain in control executing associated application program modules in an iterative loop until some user application module detects phase end conditions and effects re-entry to the Mission Executive.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Each entry in the Sequential Control Table picks up a specific entry from the Sequential Queue Table and checks to see if it is queued-in. If the entry is queued-in, the corresponding application module is executed, and control is passed to the Periodic Processor. When the entry is not queued-in or when control is returned at the completion of periodic processing, the next control table entry in sequence is processed. After the last entry in the phase Sequential Control Table has been processed, a transfer to the beginning of the table is made and the processing procedure is repeated. This iterative loop will continue until some application module returns control to the Mission Executive at phase end.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Periodic Processor (Fig. 1-5) is entered from the Non-Interrupt Sequencer after each application module execution. The Periodic Processor is basically an executable queue/control table, the Periodic Table. This table consists of entries to time tests which provide for servicing time-dependent, periodic application modules.

The flowchart illustrates a periodic processor's execution cycle. It begins with an 'Entry' point, followed by a decision diamond 'Time Test 1 Queued-in'. If 'Yes', it proceeds to 'Time to exec. Module 1', which leads to an 'APPLICATION MODULE' (hexagon) and then 'Update Time for next Exec. of this Module' (rectangle). If 'No', it bypasses the module and goes directly to the next test. This pattern repeats for 'Time Test 2' and 'Time Test n'. Each test has a 'Yes' path to its respective 'APPLICATION MODULE' and 'Update Time' step, and a 'No' path that joins the flow before the next test. A break symbol (//) indicates the loop continues for multiple tests. The process concludes with a 'Return' point.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Upon entry, the first item in the queue/control table is processed. If the entry is queued-in, an associated time test is made to determine whether or not a corresponding application module is to be called. If the time test is passed, the application module is executed and time for its next execution updated. The next entry in sequence in the queue/control table is then processed in the same manner. If a table entry is queued-out, no time test or application module will be executed before proceeding to the next entry. Likewise, if a time test is not passed, the corresponding application module will not be executed before proceeding to the next table entry. Control is returned to the Non-Interrupt Sequencer after all Periodic Table entries have been processed.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Interrupt Processor services all LVDC/LVDA interrupts under four basic levels of priority as follows:

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
Level 2: External interrupts by order of assignment to the LVDA
Interrupt Storage Register (ISR).

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: These levels determine the order in which processing will occur whenever more than one interrupt requires servicing at the same time. They also indicate the degree of priority provided for associated application module processing (Level 4 is the highest priority.) See Fig. 1-6. Processing at any level may be interrupted and delayed until all required processing at the higher level is completed. All processing performed on a non-interrupt basis is effectively at level 0, the lowest priority level.

The process then branches based on whether it is a Timer 1 Interrupt. If yes, it proceeds to a join point. If no, it checks for an External or TLC Interrupt. If yes, it leads to a connector 'A'. If no, it checks for a Timer 2 Interrupt. If no, it joins the Timer 1 path. From the join point, it checks if it is a TLC Interrupt also. If yes, it joins another point. If no, it performs 'Enable TLC Interrupt (Reset INTC)', 'Read Real Time & Save', and calls the 'APPLICATION MODULE' to process 'Figure 1-7 Timer 1 Scheduler', followed by 'Restore all Return Status'. After this, it performs 'Inhibit per Normal Inhibit Status' and 'Return to Interrupted Location'. A second path starts from connector 'A', checks for a TLC Interrupt. If yes, it joins the join point. If no, it performs 'Save Return Status Data', 'Save Normal Inhibit Status', 'Modify Normal Int. Inhibit Status to all but TLC & T1', 'Inhibit Interrupts', 'Determine Which Interrupt Occurred', 'Reset Int. and Enable TLC & T1 Ints.', and calls the 'APPLICATION MODULE' to process 'Restore Normal Int. Inhibit Status', followed by 'Restore Return Status Data'. After this, it joins the join point. From the join point, it calls the 'APPLICATION MODULE' to process 'Figure 1-8 Timer 2 Scheduler', followed by 'Restore Normal Int. chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The timer schedulers also make use of a priority scheme in selecting the next application modules to be serviced by the timer interrupts. This priority scheme, however, is only in effect when at least two application modules specify identical times for use of the same timer interrupt. In this case, the latter application module will be selected.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There are two basic classes of interrupts serviced by the Interrupt Processor: program controlled interrupts and external interrupts.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There are two program controlled interrupts: Timer 1 (formerly the minor loop counter) and Timer 2 (formerly the switch selector counter). Both of these counters operate at a 492.2 microsecond rate. Timer 1 is a continuously operating or wrap-around counter which will automatically generate an interrupt every 4.032 seconds (maximum counter value) if not under program control. Timer 2 is not a wrap-around counter. It will generate an interrupt only if initiated under program control.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: These timers are used to service application modules requiring high timing accuracy on a requested or cyclic basis. The timer counters are controlled only by the system scheduler routines (one is provided for each timer) which determine when the next timer interrupts are to occur and the application modules to be serviced. The Interrupt Processor allows Timer 2 scheduling and the application modules serviced by Timer 2 to be interrupted by Timer 1. Timer 1, therefore, is intended for use by high priority functions while Timer 2 is for functions of a lower priority.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: All LVDC/LVDA interrupts other than the timer interrupts are externally controlled; i.e., the interrupts generated are a result of the occurrence of an external event or hardware malfunction. All application modules serviced by these interrupts are required to return control to the Interrupt Processor upon their completion. The Interrupt Processor will then return control to the last interrupted location.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Timer 1 interrupt is reserved for modules whose operational accuracy requirements demand stringent timing. The Timer 1 Scheduler (Fig 1-7) is

chunks.content: designed to determine which of two modules is to execute next and to schedule the Timer 1 interrupt.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Timer 1 Scheduler gives a higher priority to one module when both modules are scheduled for the same time or are late. The higher priority module (the Program Macro Definition sub-section describes the macro by which the priority is specified) is predominantly used for minor loop operations. The lower priority module is predominantly used for switch selector operations. The two application modules and/or their entry points may be changed by queuing operations from other modules.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Timer 1 Scheduler is entered from the Interrupt Processor following the execution of a Timer 1 module or from an application module whenever a Timer 1 queuing operation is performed. Upon entry, the scheduler will decide which module requires the use of the next Timer 1 interrupt. Proper linkages for the execution of the selected module by the next Timer 1 interrupt are set-up, the Timer 1 counter is loaded with the associated time-to-go, and control is returned to the Interrupt Processor.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Timer 2 Scheduler is automatically entered from the Interrupt Processor whenever any module serviced by the Timer 2 interrupt completes processing. See Fig. 1-8. It is also automatically entered whenever any Timer 2 queuing operation is performed. The Timer 2 Scheduler is basically an executable table, the Timer 2 Table. This table consists of entries to time tests which provide for servicing time-dependent priority application modules on a requested basis.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Upon entry, the scheduler first selects itself as a module to be executed four seconds later. This is done to maintain control of scheduling in case no application module requires the use of the Timer 2 interrupt within the maximum time delta (4.032 seconds) which the timer can accommodate. The scheduler then steps through the entries in the Timer 2 Table. Each queued-in time test determines whether or not the associated application module requires use of the interrupt before the currently selected module.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: If so, that module and its associated request time becomes the current selection. This process is repeated until all table entries have been checked. Linkage to the last selected module is set up for execution on the next Timer 2 interrupt. The Timer 2 counter is loaded with the associated request time, and control is returned to the calling routine.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The primary tasks of the Control Program consist of sequencing and/or scheduling the various application modules that make up the flight program. These functions are accomplished by queue/control tables set up by the programmer with the aid of system macros. (These macros are described in the Program Macro Definition sub-section). Through these tables, a mission and its operational phases can be completely defined to the Control Program. They provide the identification of functions, their associated time requirements, and initial queue (active or inactive) status. Furthermore, certain of these tables can be dynamically altered (queuing) during the program execution to reflect changing requirements due to phase-to-phase transition or as the result of external events or program calculations. The Control Program, then, directs and controls the operation of the total flight program basically through the use of master queue/control tables.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There are essentially two classes of system tables: mission tables, which are used throughout a mission, and phase tables, which are only used for a single mission phase.

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
• • The Sequential Queue Table for the Non-Interrupt Sequencer
  • • The Periodic Table for the Periodic Processor
  • • The Timer 2 Table for the Timer 2 Scheduler
  • • The Phase Selection Table for the Phase Initializer

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The first of these is a queue table and the next two are queue/control tables. This distinction is made because of the manner in which the tables are used. Queueing may be performed in these three tables but only the Periodic and the Timer 2 Tables are directly executed to provide control. The Sequential Queue Table is used as data by the phase Sequential Control Tables and is not directly executed. The last table, the Phase Selection Table, is neither queued nor executed but provides control variables and constants for each mission phase. *

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There is only one type of phase table, the Sequential Control Table. However, there is a Sequential Control Table for each phase of the mission. Note that the term "control table" is used in keeping with the previous nomenclature convention. These tables cannot be queued but are directly executed to provide control.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Sequential Queue Table (Table 1-1) consists of instructions which address the various sequential application modules to be executed. One entry is required for each module to be sequenced regardless of the number of phases in which sequencing is to be performed. The system provides for a maximum of 200 entries in this table. The order of the entries is irrelevant. Queueing is performed by altering the instruction operation code in the desired table entry.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The queue/control tables for the Periodic Processor (Table 1-2) and the Timer 2 Scheduler (Table 1-3) are essentially alike. They differ only in the form of their respective time tests and will therefore be discussed together. Each entry consists of a linkage to a corresponding time test for the scheduling of time dependent application modules. One entry is required for each module to be scheduled. The system allows a maximum of 25 entries in each table. Again, queueing is accomplished by the alteration of the operation code in the desired table entry. Note that in these tables only a time test is being queued, not an actual application module.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: A distinction regarding the ordering of entries does exist between the Periodic and the Timer 2 Tables. In the Periodic Processor, an application module is called directly by its associated time test (assuming that test was queued-in and that the time test was passed). This imparts a priority to the entries in the Periodic Table; the order of the entries in the table implies their priority of execution. In the Timer 2 Scheduler, the order of entries is somewhat irrelevant. The queued-in time tests select the application module (or the scheduler itself) to be executed next, strictly as a function of time. However, if two or more modules request simultaneous execution, the last module tested will be serviced first.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Phase Selection Table (Table 1-4) is generated as a by-product of the system macros and provides information for the initialization of each mission phase. Entries are made in the order in which the corresponding phases are to be executed.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: These tables (see Table 1-5 for table format) consist of two instructions for each entry. The first instruction addresses a particular entry from the Sequential Queue Table. The second instruction is identical for all entries; it is linkage to a system subroutine. Essentially, the subroutine uses the entry from the queue table to determine whether or not the associated application module is to be executed.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: A Sequential Control Table for any particular mission phase will contain at least one entry for each application module to be handled by the Non-Interrupt Sequencer during that phase. Multiple entries for a particular module can be used to provide a higher frequency (relative to the other modules) of execution for that module. Note that a priority is implied by the order of the entries in the Sequential Control Tables. The system will permit a maximum of 50 entries in each of these tables.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Flexibility is the primary reason for the multiple-table design of the Non-Interrupt Sequencer. The control tables provide the capability for altering the sequence of execution of application modules from phase to phase while the master queue tables provide the uniform queuing base for all phases.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: A common communications area, the data pack, is provided in order to centralize all data communications between application modules and between the Control Program and application modules. The data pack identifies and defines all data used by the flight program. It is organized into groups segmenting telemetry identification, pseudo variables, data definitions, and table definitions.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Data which are to be telemetered are identified in a telemetry table via the TELD macro stating the data name, the mode setting, and the PIO tag. Actual data definition and memory address assignments are not done at this point but are included in the appropriate function data definition group.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: All vehicle or mission dependent data parameters are defined by means of the "pseudo-variable" capability of the LVDC Assembler. This allows module operation to be independent of these change prone variables and constants. Also, status words, conversion factors, and certain control words are defined as pseudo variables. All left-hand labels for pseudo-variables begin with 'P.'. For example, P.M1 is the label of the pseudo-variable representing the mass of the vehicle at liftoff used to compute (F/M)_c.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Data definitions include targeting parameters, utility data, control data, and module associated data. Assignments to residual storage are based on number of references in order to conserve storage. Module associated data are grouped to identify data common to a small group of modules. Data definitions unique to individual modules are also isolated. Data definition labels begin with 'D.', 'V.', 'L.', 'F.', 'G.', or 'H.'. *

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Table definitions include such tables as Switch Selector Tables, Event Processor Tables, and Ladder Ramp Tables.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: An application module is defined as a program unit exclusively designed and tailored to perform one or a number of related functions, i.e., each application module is function-oriented. The application module concept is intended to provide a source pool of program modules which can be used to generate different flight program configurations for any number of missions.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Module execution is governed by the Control Program either directly (the module is called by the Control Program) or indirectly (the module is called as a subroutine by another module already under direct control of the Control Program). When called, each module will perform its unique function and return control to the calling source. All inter-module communication, and all queuing of modules is to be accomplished through the system macros.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Two system macros are provided for modules to specify the queue status of a module and, if applicable, the time or rate of execution for that module. The E.QT macro specifies the time or rate of execution, and the E.Q macro sets the queue status of a module.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The E.QT macro is not valid for queuing Non-Interrupt Sequencer modules since their operation is cyclic rather than time associated. The time given in the E.QT macro for Periodic Processor modules is an execution rate. A module that is queued-in will be executed at the time interval specified. The time specified for Timer 1 and Timer 2 modules indicates a specific time the module is to be executed. When a Timer 1 or Timer 2 module gains control, it must reschedule itself or queue itself out before returning control to the Control Program.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: For queuing Timer 1 modules only, the E.QT macro also queues-in the specified module. Timer 1 modules are queued-out indirectly by queuing-in another module via the E.QT macro or by specifying a time to execute which will never be reached.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The E.Q macro is used for queuing Non-Interrupt Sequencer, Periodic Processor, and Timer 2 modules. A time or rate of execution must be

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: specified for Periodic Processor and Timer 2 modules before the E.Q macro is used. The E.Q macro is invalid for Timer 1 modules. Table 1-6 summarizes the queuing functions for the different classes.

chunks.label: Table
chunks.content:
Macro Non-Interrupt Sequencer Modules Periodic Processor Modules Timer 2 Modules Timer 1 Modules
E.QT Invalid Specifies rate of execution Specifies time of execution Specifies time of execution and queues-in
E.Q. Queues-In/Out Queues-In/Out Queues-In/Out Invalid

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The flight program is composed of the Control Program, the common communications area, and all of the application modules described in the Application Modules Description section. The configuration of the flight program is defined by the flight programmer via system macros. The macros define those modules which will execute under direct control of the Control Program and the controlling component under which each will execute.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There are three categories of program definition macros. Mission macros provide module definitions and certain control information for the entire mission. Phase macros define the functions for each program phase. Interrupt macros provide the control information for interrupt processing.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The macro program definition is expected to remain relatively consistent from flight to flight, but new requirements may result in timing differences or in changing modules. Part IV will define the individual program definition when it varies from that specified in Table 1-7. The following paragraphs describe the three macro categories.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There is one group of mission macros beginning with the E.MIN macro and ending with the E.MEND macro. This group must precede the other groups. Macros in this group define all modules (their entry points) which will execute under direct control of the Control Program during the mission and the controlling sub-program under which each will execute. In addition, the execution rate for those modules which will be controlled by the Periodic Processor are defined.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The queue status of all Timer 2 modules will be set as queued-in. The queue status can be overridden by the phase definition macros for the phase(s) in which the module is to execute or by another module. The queue status of the Non-Interrupt Sequencer modules is not defined via the mission macros since there is a separate control table for each phase. The Sequential Queue Table, the Periodic Table, and the Timer 2 Table are allocated as a result of these macros.

chunks.label: Diagram
chunks.content:
The flowchart is divided into two main sections: Phase 1 Non-Interrupt Sequencer (left) and a subsequent section (right). Both sections follow a similar pattern of decision-making based on module queuing status.

Phase 1 Non-Interrupt Sequencer (Left Section):

  • ACCELER-OMETER READ (AR): Always queued-in. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → AR; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • SIMULATED ACCELER-OMETERS (SA): Always queued-out in Flight Mode. In Flight Simulation, always queued-in. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → SA; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • DISCRETE PROCESSOR (DP): Always queued-in in Flight Mode and Non-Repeatable Mode. Always queued-out in Repeatable Mode. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → DP; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • ACCELER-OMETER PROCESSING (AP): Always queued-in. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → AP; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • F/M CALCULATIONS (DV): Queued-in by Events Processor based on mission dependent times. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → DV; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • BOOST NAVIGATION (NE): Always queued-in. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → NE; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • PHASE ACTIVATOR (PA): Queued-in once by Events Processor to terminate Phase 1 & initiate Phase 2. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → PA; No → RS 1 → Decision.
  • TIME TILT GUIDANCE (TT): Queued-in Phase 1 by Events Processor at a preset time in TB1 and queues itself out when tilt arrest time is reached. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → TT; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • CHI COMPUTATIONS (CC): Queued-in by Time Tilt and Events Processor and queued-out by Events Processor. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → CC; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.

Right Section:

  • IGM (IG): Queued-in by Events Processor at preset time in TB3. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → IGM; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • S-IVB CUTOFF PREDICTION (HS): Queued-in when predicted time-to-go to S-IVB cutoff is less than a preset value. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → HS; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • ORBIT GUIDANCE (OG): Queued-in by Events Processor in Phase 1. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → OG; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • TIME BASE 4 (TB4): Queued-in by Events Processor at preset time in TB3. Queued-out upon setting TB4. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → TB4; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • MINOR LOOP SUPPORT (NS): Always queued-in in Flight Mode. In Flight Simulation, always queued-out. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → NS; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • APS ATTITUDE CONTROL TEST (AC): Queued-in by Events Processor at preset time in TB5. Queued-out at TB5, upon failure of the test, or upon acceptance of the LML DCS Command. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → AC; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • SIMULATED PLATFORM GIMBAL ANGLES (PG): Always queued-out in Flight Mode. In Flight Simulation always queued-in. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → PG; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.
  • ETC/BTC (EB): Always queued-in. Decision: Module Queued-in? Yes → EB; No → Periodic Processor → Fig. 1-9c → Decision.

The flowchart concludes with a return to NS 2 at the bottom.

chunks.label: Diagram
chunks.content:
The flowchart illustrates the general flow of the Saturn IB Flight Program, specifically focusing on interrupt processing and task scheduling. It is divided into two main sections: the Interrupt Processor and the Timer Interrupt Processor.

Interrupt Processor:

  • Interrupt Entry: The process begins at the 'Interrupt Entry' point.
  • Timer 1 Interrupt:
    • If Yes, it proceeds to MINOR LOOP (ML) (In Phase 1, executed every 40 ms. In Phase 2, executes every 100 ms.) and LIFTOFF SEARCH (LO) (Queued-in by Events Processor at GRR + sec. Queued-out when Liftoff is detected. While queued-in, accesses Minor Loop to maintain its 40 ms. execution rate.) and SWITCH SELECTOR PROCESSING (SS) (Sequential entries are scheduled in the process of issuing a switch selector.)
    • If No, it proceeds to TLC Interrupt.
  • TLC Interrupt:
    • If Yes, it proceeds to SIMULTANEOUS MEMORY ERROR RECOVERY (TS) (Executes on occurrence of a TLC interrupt. Exits to Interrupt Processor or Phase Activator.) and then ERROR RECOVERY EXIT.
    • If No, it proceeds to External Interrupt.
  • External Interrupt:
    • If Yes, it proceeds to DIGITAL COMMAND SYSTEM (DS) (Executes when a valid command is received during specified time frames.) and TIME BASE 3 (TB3) (Executes on occurrence of S-IB Propellant Depletion Interrupt.)
    • If No, it proceeds to TIME BASE 4 (TB4) (Executes on occurrence of S-IVB Engine Out Interrupt.) and TIME BASE 2 (TB2) (Executes on occurrence of S-IB Low Level Sense Interrupts.)
  • Return to Interrupted Location: After processing, the flow returns to the RETURN TO INTERRUPTED LOCATION point.

Timer Interrupt Processor:

  • Timer 2 Interrupt:
    • If Yes, it proceeds to PHASE I TIME UPDATE (UM) (Executes every 0.8 seconds in Phase 1. Queued-out during Phase 2.) and LADDER RAMP PROCESSOR (LR) (Always queued-out in Flight Mode. Only executes in Flight Simulation Mode.) and EVENTS PROCESSOR (EP) (Always queued-in. Schedules itself at specific times in order to perform tasks which are a function of time.)
    • If No, it proceeds to NAVIGATION UPDATE IMPLEMENTATION (NU) (Scheduled by DCS.) and PHASE II CONTROL (CM) (Three entries are scheduled (with offsets) at 8 sec, 8 sec, and 1 sec intervals during Phase 2.)
    • WATER VALVE ACTIVATE (WM) (Queued-in in Phases I and II unless queued-out by DCS in Phase II.)
    • ORBITAL GUIDANCE MANEUVER PROCESSOR (MP) (Queued-in during Phase I and II. Scheduled as a function of time for nominal maneuver initiation by DCS.)
    • TIME BASE 5 START (TB5) (Scheduled by DCS.)
    • TB5 ALT SEQUENCE REQUEST (AS) (Scheduled by Time Base 5 Start Logic or itself.)
  • Scheduling Logic:
    • Select and Schedule Next Module for Timer 1 Interrupt: Receives input from the Interrupt Processor and the Timer Interrupt Processor.
    • Select and Schedule Next Module for Timer 2 Interrupt: Receives input from the Timer Interrupt Processor.
  • Return to Interrupted Location: After scheduling, the flow returns to the RETURN TO INTERRUPTED LOCATION point.

Annotations and Connections:

  • TIS: A connection point between the Interrupt Processor and the Timer Interrupt Processor.
  • Point A: A connection point at the top and bottom of the flowchart, indicating a loop or return to the start.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: This section describes the implementation of each application module in the Saturn IB Flight Program. If the implementation of a module varies because of a specific flight's requirements, that module will be described in the appropriate section of Part IV.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The module flowcharts are written in prose for better understanding of the operations performed and decisions made. Since these flowcharts are generated from the program listing, it is very easy to correlate the programming instructions to the flowchart. The hierarchy of flowcharts allows a reader to gain an overview of the module's operation from the first level and more detail from the subsequent levels.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The programming notes which support the flowcharts define all intermodule linkages, telemetry data, and initial conditions. The flowcharts show all external module linkages except for certain utility routines used in computing equations. The programming notes include all external linkages as well as system macros. All system macros begin with "E." as well as Control Program subroutines which can be accessed by modules. In their expansion, the following system macros access Control Program subroutines:

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: E.ENBL      System macro to restore the normal LVDC interrupt status by providing linkage which transfers control to the executive interrupt enable subroutine which, in turn, reloads the inhibit register with the normal inhibits associated with the processing level in progress and returns control to the user.

chunks.label: Table
chunks.content:
E.MPP System macro for generating an entry in the Periodic Processor queue table.
E.MT2S System macro for generating an entry in the Timer 2 Scheduler queue/control table.
E.PEND System macro for the termination of the phase table information.
E.PIN System macro for initialization required prior to generation of Phase Table information.

The flowchart, titled "ACCELEROMETER PROCESSING (AP)", details the following steps:

  • START AP101: Initiates the process.
  • SET PREV. DELTA VELOCITY WORD TO ZERO: Prepares the velocity word for the next step.
  • EST. THRUST MISALIGN ERROR IN COMP. OF F/M FO.4.2.3: Estimates the thrust misalignment error.
  • AP400 AO: SELECT A OR B X ACCEL CHANGE: Selects between two acceleration change options.
  • DID DELTA PASS ZERO TEST: A decision point. If NO, it proceeds to AP130. If YES, it proceeds to AP500 AO: MAKE RSINS TEST ON DEL X ACCEL CHG.
  • AP500 AO: MAKE RSINS TEST ON DEL X ACCEL CHG: Performs a test on the delta X acceleration change.
  • AP116: A processing block that leads to AP110.
  • AP110: A processing block that leads to AP120.
  • AP120: A processing block that leads to SET STEERING MISALIGNMENT INHIBIT FLAG.
  • SET STEERING MISALIGNMENT INHIBIT FLAG: Sets the steering misalignment inhibit flag.
  • Determine Biased Backup Velocity: Determines the biased backup velocity.
  • AP150: A processing block that leads to CALCULATE X VELOCITY FO.4.2.7.
  • CALCULATE X VELOCITY FO.4.2.7: Calculates the X velocity.
  • T0-T000 TELM MEAS. VELOCITY OF PLATFORM AXIS X: Measures the velocity of the platform axis.
  • EXIT AP200: Terminates the process.
  • AP130: A decision point. If YES, it leads to AP110. If NO, it leads to AP120.
  • AP116: A decision point. If YES, it leads to AP140. If NO, it leads to AP120.
  • AP140: A processing block that leads to AP600 CO: ACCUMULATE SQUARE OF ACCEL CHANGES.
  • AP600 CO: ACCUMULATE SQUARE OF ACCEL CHANGES: Accumulates the square of acceleration changes.
  • AP120: A decision point. If YES, it leads to AP110. If NO, it leads to AP120.
  • AP120: A processing block that leads to SET MORE CODE 24 BOTH X READS FAILED.
  • SET MORE CODE 24 BOTH X READS FAILED: Sets the more code 24 for both X reads failed.

The flowchart describes the following steps:

  • START AP201: Initial start point.
  • AP400 AO. SELECT A OR B Y ACCEL CHANGE: Selects between acceleration modes A or B.
  • DID DELTA PASS ZERO TEST: Checks if the delta acceleration is zero.
    • If NO, it proceeds to EXPECTED CHANGE <THRUST MISALIGN ERROR.
    • If YES, it proceeds to MAKE RESINS TEST ON DEL Y ACCEL CHG.
  • EXPECTED CHANGE <THRUST MISALIGN ERROR: Checks for expected changes.
    • If YES, it proceeds to MAKE RESINS TEST ON DEL Y ACCEL CHG.
    • If NO, it proceeds to SET MODE CODE 24 Y ACCEL ZERO FAILURE.
  • MAKE RESINS TEST ON DEL Y ACCEL CHG: Tests the delta acceleration with resins.
  • DID DELTA PASS RESINS TEST: Checks if the test with resins passed.
    • If YES, it proceeds to SET MODE CODE 24 Y ACCEL ZERO FAILURE.
    • If NO, it proceeds to SET MODE CODE 24 BTH RESINS FAILED.
  • SET MODE CODE 24 Y ACCEL ZERO FAILURE: Sets the mode code for zero failure.
  • SET MODE CODE 24 BTH RESINS FAILED: Sets the mode code for failed resins.
  • SET STEERING MISALIGNMENT INHIBIT FLAG: Sets a flag to inhibit steering misalignment.
  • DETERMINE BIASED Y BACKUP VELOCITY: Determines the biased Y backup velocity.
  • CALCULATE Y VELOCITY EQ. 4.2.7: Calculates the Y velocity using equation 4.2.7.
  • TELEM MEAS VELOCITY OF PLATFORM AXIS: Telematics measure the velocity of the platform axis.
  • EXIT AP300: Final exit point.

A decision point "AP450: DELTA A & B AGREE WITHIN 2 PULSES" follows. If "YES", it leads to a block labeled "B4". If "NO", it goes to "DELTA A CLOSEST TO PREDICTED CHANGE".   • A vertical connector leads to a decision diamond: IS THE EXPECTED CHANGE LT ZERO.
  • If YES, it leads to a vertical connector.
  • If NO, it leads to a decision diamond: DELTA GT 1.5*EXP VEL CHG+RTC EQ.4-2.4.
  • If YES, it leads to a vertical connector.
  • If NO, it leads to a decision diamond: DELTA GT 5*EXP VEL CHG+RTC EQ.4-2.4.
  • If YES, it leads to AP510 (text).
  • AP510 leads to EXIT DELTA REASONABLE (dotted box).
  • If NO, it leads to AP520 (text).
  • AP520 leads to a decision diamond: DELTA GT 5*EXP VEL CHG+RTC EQ.4-2.5.
  • If YES, it leads to AP510.
  • If NO, it leads to AP530 (text).
  • AP530 leads to EXIT DELTA NOT REASONABLE (dotted box).
  • There is a feedback loop from the YES path of the first decision diamond back to the NO path of the second decision diamond.

AP600 Path:

  • START AP600 (dotted box) leads to a vertical connector.
  • The connector leads to ACCUMULATE SQUARED VELOCITY (text).
  • A vertical connector leads to a dotted box: SQUARE VELOCITY CHANGE (X,Y, OR Z).
  • A vertical connector leads to a dotted box: ACCUMULATE SQUARED ACCELEROMETER CHANGES.
  • A vertical connector leads to EXIT RETURN (dotted box).

chunks.content: The previous accelerometer readings (V.OACX, V.OACY, and V.OACZ) will be initialized by the Control Program at GRR. D.VFOM is initialized to (P.FOVO).

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Interrupts are inhibited across accelerometer and real time clock reads, calculations of time in mission (D.VTAS), time in time base (D.VTB), computation cycle length (D.VDT), the resetting of Mode Code 24 (D.VMC4) and the use of D.VFOR (Force), D.VMAS (Mass), D.VMFR (Mass flow rate) and D.VPF (performance factor) in the backup acceleration computations.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Average pitch and yaw Minor Loop command chi's are calculated in the Accelerometer Read module for use in computing the steering misalignment correction terms. These angles are calculated at this time to synch them with the accelerometer readings.

chunks.content:
graph TD; A[START A4+1] --> B[CALCULATE AVERAGE YAW COMMAND CHI]; B --> C[RESET YAW COMMAND CHI FOR NEXT PASS]; C --> D[CALCULATE AVERAGE PITCH COMMAND CHI]; D --> E{PRESENT - PAST PITCH COMMAND GT 50 DEGS}; E -- YES --> F[ADD 130 DEG TO THE AVER PITCH COMMAND CHI]; E -- NO --> G[RESET PAST PITCH COMMAND CHI FOR NEXT PASS]; F --> G; G --> H[EXIT A054];

The flowchart, titled "ACCELEROMETER READ (AP)", describes a process for calculating and updating yaw and pitch commands. It begins with a "START A4+1" block, followed by "CALCULATE AVERAGE YAW COMMAND CHI", then "RESET YAW COMMAND CHI FOR NEXT PASS". Next is "CALCULATE AVERAGE PITCH COMMAND CHI", leading to a decision diamond: "PRESENT - PAST PITCH COMMAND GT 50 DEGS". If "YES", it proceeds to "ADD 130 DEG TO THE AVER PITCH COMMAND CHI". If "NO", it goes to "RESET PAST PITCH COMMAND CHI FOR NEXT PASS". Both paths then lead to "RESET PAST PITCH COMMAND CHI FOR NEXT PASS", which finally leads to "EXIT A054". A label "AR50" is positioned to the left of the "RESET PAST PITCH COMMAND CHI FOR NEXT PASS" block.

graph TD
        StartAR65C[START AR65C] --> IsTimeBaseSet{IS TIME BASE SET}
        IsTimeBaseSet -- YES --> ComputeFMI[COMPUTE (F/M)IC EQ.4-2-12]
        IsTimeBaseSet -- NO --> ExitAR82[EXIT AR82]
        ComputeFMI --> ExitAR82
        
        FirstPassAR80C{FIRST PASS AFTER THRUST CHANGE EVENT} -- YES --> TimeForNewThrust{TIME FOR NEW THRUST EVENT PARAMETERS}
        FirstPassAR80C -- NO --> EnableInt[AR81 (E,ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS]
        TimeForNewThrust -- YES --> ChangeThrust[CHANGE THRUST EVENT PARAMETERS]
        TimeForNewThrust -- NO --> EnableInt
        ChangeThrust --> ComputeFMI[COMPUTE (F/M)IC USING EQ.4-2-17 THRU EQ.4-2-22]
        ComputeFMI --> ResetThrust[RESET THRUST CHANGE EVENT FLAG]
        ResetThrust --> ComputeDelta[COMPUTE DELTA T FVNT EQ.4-2-19]
        ComputeDelta --> ComputeCurrent[COMPUTE CURRENT BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-17]
        ComputeCurrent --> MassChanged{MASS CHANGED AT THRUST EVENT}
        MassChanged -- YES --> SetM1[SET M1C1 = M(T)]
        MassChanged -- NO --> ComputeAvg[COMPUTE AVG MASS PRIOR TO EVENT EQ.4-2-18]
        SetM1 --> ComputeAvg
        ComputeAvg --> ExitAR82[EXIT AR82]
        
        InFlightMode{IN FLIGHT MODE} -- YES --> InTimeBase{IN TIME BASE}
        InTimeBase -- YES --> TimeToChange{TIME TO CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR}
        TimeToChange -- YES --> ChangeMisalign[AR72 CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR]
        TimeToChange -- NO --> ComputeFMI[COMPUTE (F/M)IC EQ.4-2-15]
        InFlightMode -- NO --> ComputeFMI
        ChangeMisalign --> EnableInt
        EnableInt --> ComputePrev[COMPUTE PREVIOUS UPDATED BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-13]
        ComputePrev --> ComputeAvg[COMPUTE THE AVERAGE BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-14]
        ComputeAvg --> ComputeFMI
        ComputeFMI --> ExitAR82

The flowchart is titled "ACCELEROMETER READ (AR)". It begins with a "START AR65C" block. A decision diamond "IS TIME BASE SET" follows. If "YES", it proceeds to "COMPUTE (F/M)IC EQ.4-2-12" and then "EXIT AR82". If "NO", it goes directly to "EXIT AR82".

Next is a decision diamond "FIRST PASS AFTER THRUST CHANGE EVENT". If "YES", it goes to "TIME FOR NEW THRUST EVENT PARAMETERS". If "NO", it goes to "AR81 (E,ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS".

"TIME FOR NEW THRUST EVENT PARAMETERS" has two paths: "YES" leads to "CHANGE THRUST EVENT PARAMETERS" and then "COMPUTE (F/M)IC USING EQ.4-2-17 THRU EQ.4-2-22"; "NO" leads to "AR81 (E,ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS".

"CHANGE THRUST EVENT PARAMETERS" leads to "RESET THRUST CHANGE EVENT FLAG", which then leads to "COMPUTE DELTA T FVNT EQ.4-2-19", "COMPUTE CURRENT BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-17", and a decision diamond "MASS CHANGED AT THRUST EVENT". If "YES", it goes to "SET M1C1 = M(T)" and then "COMPUTE AVG MASS PRIOR TO EVENT EQ.4-2-18", finally "EXIT AR82". If "NO", it goes directly to "COMPUTE AVG MASS PRIOR TO EVENT EQ.4-2-18".

"AR81 (E,ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS" leads to "COMPUTE (F/M)IC USING EQ.4-2-13 THRU EQ.4-2-15", "COMPUTE CURRENT BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-13", "COMPUTE PREVIOUS UPDATED BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-12-1", "COMPUTE THE AVERAGE BACKUP MASS EQ.4-2-14", and "COMPUTE (F/M)IC EQ.4-2-15", all leading to "EXIT AR82".

There are also several other paths: "IN FLIGHT MODE" leads to "IN TIME BASE", "TIME TO CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR", and "CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR" (labeled AR72). "IN TIME BASE" leads to "TIME TO CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR". "TIME TO CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR" leads to "CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR" (labeled AR72) and "COMPUTE (F/M)IC EQ.4-2-15". "CHANGE THRUST MISALIGNMENT VECTOR" leads to "AR80 (E,IMBT) INHIBIT INTERRUPTS" and "AR80C". "AR80C" leads to "AR81 (E,ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS", which leads to "EXIT AR82".

chunks.content: M.AS00 Entered from Timer 2 when scheduled by either the Time Base 5 start logic or itself.

chunks.label: Text

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VTLD Duration time of LOX dump included in De-Orbit command

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VTHD Duration time of LH2 dump included in De-Orbit command

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: F.SRW must be zero on first entry to obtain proper order of dump sequences. *

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The function of the Arctangent Utility module is to compute the arctangent of the quotient of two specified numbers by means of an algorithm which utilizes a polynomial approximation to the arctangent function.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: On entry the accumulator must contain the sine of the desired angle (ARG1) and the PQ register must contain the cosine of the desired angle (ARG2).

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Upon exit the desired angle, \arctan(\text{ARG1}/\text{ARG2}), will be in the accumulator in pirads scaled B0.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Phase II Control module maintains the navigation and guidance timeline for the orbital phases of operation, Phase 2.

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
• M.CM00 Entered from Timer 2 every eight seconds during Phase 2 for navigation processing.
  • M.CM01 Entered by the Navigation Update Implementation module when a DCS update has been processed for navigation processing. Control is returned to Timer 2 rather than the module.
  • M.CM10 Entered from Timer 2 every eight seconds during Phase 2 for saving guidance chi's and total gimbals for midpoint navigation processing.
  • M.CM20 Entered from Timer 2 every second between navigation (M.CM00) entries for guidance processing.

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
• M.DP00 Discrete Processor
  • M.EB10 ETC/BTC
  • M.EC00 Minor Loop Error Monitor
  • M.GL00 Acquisition Gain/Loss
  • M.MS00 Minor Loop Support
  • M.NI00 Navigation Extrapolation
  • M.NZ00 Orbit Navigation
  • M.OG00 Orbit Guidance
  • M.PA00 Phase Activator
  • M.PC01 One second Data Compression
  • M.OV00 Orbit Velocity Calculations
  • M.AC00 APS Attitude Control Test

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The scheduled times for the three entries, D.VT8S, D.VT4S, and D.VT1S, are set to phase start plus 8, 4, and 1 seconds respectively.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Although both entries M.CM00 and M.CM10 have an eight second rate, they are scheduled so that there is a four second off-set between entering M.CM00 and M.CM10.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: In Flight Simulation Mode, the guidance chi's are used for midpoint navigation gimbals. In Flight Mode, the actual gimbals are used.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: In Flight Simulation Mode, the Simulated Platform Gimbal Angles module will be executed instead of the Minor Loop Support module. The Simulated Platform Gimbal Angles module is not executed in the Flight Mode.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Phase Activator module is given control when the phase is to be terminated. Control is not returned to the Phase II Control module.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The function of the Cutoff Logic module is to provide the capability for accurately issuing S-IVB cutoff.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: M.CO00 Entered via Minor Loop when S-IVB cutoff is imminent.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
E.GP07Timer 2 Halt and Reschedule*
E.GP20Control Program Time Update*
H.S027High Speed Loop S-IVB cutoff switch selector read issuance
E.IHBTInhibit interrupts
E.QS-IVB Cutoff Prediction (M.HS00)
E.QTSwitch Selector Processing (M.SS60)
E.QTEvents Processor (M.EP00)

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.VCORRTC read associated with D.VTMS
D.VTMMElapsed time in mission from GRR to last time update*
D.VTMSCurrent time-to-go to S-IVB cutoff*
D.VTRRElapsed total time in current time base*
V.YAWActual yaw ladder command
V.PITActual pitch ladder command
V.ROLActual roll ladder command

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.VMLTExecution time of next Minor Loop
D.VTBIIndication of time base initiation*

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.VTMS Current time-to-go to S-IVB cutoff
D.GMLC Variable HOP constant to M.C000 or M.L299

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.FILE Flight Program Status
D.FIL3 Timer 1 interrupt in progress indicator
D.FIL2 External int level in progress indicator
D.VMC5 Mode Code 25

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: To insure accurate issuance of S-IVB cutoff and to maintain the proper minor loop rate, the Cutoff Logic module will be called as a special subroutine of the Minor Loop module. To activate this module, the HOP Constant D.GMLC must be set to M.C000. This module will deactivate itself by resetting D.GMLC to M.L299 after the S-IVB cutoff switch selector read has been issued.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: This module serves as the active major loop after there has been a Compressed Data Dump DCS command. The module telemeters different types of data which have been stored from the previous dark period and/or which are sampled at known intervals. These data are telemetered from predefined data tables with each having its own associated PIO tag.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: M.CT00 Entered from the Non-Interrupt Sequencer once per computation cycle during Phase 2 when queued-in by the Compressed Data Dump DCS command.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
U.TR00 Real Time Telemetry Delay Utility
E.Q Compressed Data Telemetry (M.CT00)
E.IHBT Inhibit interrupts
E.ENBL Enable interrupts

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
V.KSTR Compressed data storage flag
D.BPT1 Table 1 beginning pointer
D.BPT2 Table 2 beginning pointer
D.BPT3 Table 3 beginning pointer
D.BPT4 Table 4 beginning pointer
D.EPT1 Table 1 ending pointer
D.EPT2 Table 2 ending pointer
D.EPT3 Table 3 ending pointer
D.EPT4 Table 4 ending pointer
D.PPT1 Table 1 present pointer
D.PPT2 Table 2 present pointer

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.PPT3 Table 3 present pointer
D.PPT4 Table 4 present pointer
D.FDTL Memory dump/compressed data dump in progress flag *

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.VER8 Accumulated eight second composite EMR word *
F.EMR8 Dark period EMR accumulation flag *

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
Compressed Data Table 1
Compressed Data Table 2
Compressed Data Table 3
Compressed Data Table 4

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.PPT1, ..., D.PPT4 must be set to D.EPT1, ..., D.EPT4, respectively.
V.ECT1, ..., V.ECT4 must be set to V.ECK1, ..., V.ECK4, respectively.
V.FPIO must be non-zero.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: There are four telemetry tables. This module telemeters one entry from each table each computation cycle in such a manner that each table is completely telemetered once before beginning telemetry of any table a second time and each table is completely telemetered twice before beginning telemetry of any table a third time. Each table begins at corresponding locations in different data sectors so that the selection of a table is made by changing data sectors.

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
• o Telemetry Table 1: Contains 3 fine gimbal angles and time and 3 backup gimbal angles and time. Eight words per entry. PIO Tag 3404.
  • o Telemetry Table 2: Contains the 60 second composite EMR word and time. Two words per entry. PIO Tag 3414.
  • o Telemetry Table 3: Contains 3 accelerometers and time. Four words per entry. PIO Tag 3410.
  • o Telemetry Table 4: Contains MC24 and time, TLC and time, switch selector and time, DIN's and time, etc. Two words per entry. PIO Tag 3041.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: This module queues itself out when each compressed data table has been completely telemetered three times or is queued out by the DCS module (DS) upon receipt of a Terminate DCS command.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The flag V.KSTR must be set non-zero in the Flight Mode to indicate data compression is active. In the Flight Simulation Mode, the flag is set according to the Flight Simulator Indicator request for data compression.

The flowchart describes the logic for the COMPRESSED DATA TELEMETRY (CT) module. It begins with a start point 'M.CT00'. The first decision is 'COMPRESSED DATA TELEMETRY ACTIVE'. If 'NO', it sets register 'B6.' to a specific value. If 'YES', it checks for a 'NEW DUMP REQUESTED'. If 'YES', it sets the 'MEM/COMP DATA DUMP IN PROGRESS FLAG' and proceeds to 'CT001'. If 'NO', it checks 'DUMP IN PROGRESS'. If 'YES', it proceeds to 'CT001'. If 'NO', it exits to 'EXIT RETURN'. 'CT001' checks if 'ALL TABLES COMPLETELY TELEMETRED'. If 'NO', it sets 'CT10' to '2 60.' and proceeds to 'TELEMETRED ENTRY FROM ALL FOUR TABLES'. If 'YES', it decrements the 'COMPLETE TABLE TELE-COUNTER'. This leads to a check 'ALL TABLES TELEMETRED TIMES 3'. If 'NO', it sets register 'C1.' to a specific value. If 'YES', it sets register 'B6.' to a specific value and proceeds to '(E.IHBT) INHIBIT INTERRUPTS'. This is followed by '(E.Q) O-OUT COMPRESSED TELEMETRY (M.CT00)', then 'ZERO DARK PERIOD EMR WORD', 'ENABLE MEM/COMP DATA DUMP DCS COMMANDS', '(E.ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS', and 'C.T98', all leading to 'EXIT RETURN'. The 'TELEMETRED ENTRY FROM ALL FOUR TABLES' decision also leads to 'EXIT RETURN' if 'YES', or to 'ALTER HPC TO SELECT NEXT TABLE' (setting 'C3.') if 'NO', which then loops back to 'CT10'.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The function of the Disagreement Bit Processing module is to determine the conditions under which LVDA hardware logic has set the disagreement bit and to select a good resolver for minor loop processing.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: M.DG00 Entered from the Minor Loop module for all axes.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VDGS Count of failures in disagreement bit circuitry

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.GMLT HOP constant to telemetry delay or telemetry bypass

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VAFR Count of times A resolver determined bad

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VBFR Count of times B resolver determined bad

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VABF Count of times A & B resolvers determined bad

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VHDB Count of times B multiplexer circuitry defective

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VDGS Count of failures in disagreement bit circuitry

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VAFR Count of times A resolver determined bad

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VBFR Count of times B resolver determined bad

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VABF Count of times A & B resolvers determined bad

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: D.VHDB Count of times B multiplexer circuitry defective

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The following items are to be initialized at mission start:

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content:
D.VDGS Count of failures in disagreement bit circuitry
D.VAFR Count of times A resolver determined bad
D.VBFR Count of times B resolver determined bad
D.VABF Count of times A & B resolvers determined bad
D.VHDB Count of times B multiplexer circuitry defective

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Disagreement Bit Processing module has three unique exits to indicate the results of its processing. Control is returned to one of the three instruction locations following the HOP instruction to M.DG00 as follows:

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Exit 1: Either a cross over of the gimbals caused the DB to be set or a hardware DB circuitry set the DB invalidly. The gimbal is to be used for processing of the actual attitude.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Exit 2: No valid counter was found by using the test counters.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: Exit 3: A valid counter was found when the test counters were checked.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The good counter is to be used for processing of the actual attitude.

The flowchart, titled "CISAGREEMENT BIT PROCESSING (DG)", begins with a "START M.DG00" block. It proceeds to "D0000 DETERMINE A AND B COUNTER DIFFERENCE". From there, it reaches a decision point "D0005 DB DUE TO CROSSOVER". If "NO", it goes to "D0010 INCREMENT CIRCUTRY FAILURE COUNT". If "YES", it also goes to "D0010". From "D0010", the flow goes to "D0010 (U,TROO) TELEM ERROR WORD (DB CIR FAILURE)", then to "D0010 USE A COUNTER VALUE", and finally to "EXIT RETURN". Alternatively, from "D0005", if "NO", it goes to "D0100 COUNTER TESTS", which then leads to "D0600 WERE BOTH COUNTERS GOOD". If "YES", it goes to "EXIT RETURN". If "NO", it goes to "D0410 SET MULTIPLEXER FAILURE", which then leads to "EXIT RETURN".

The flowchart is titled "DISCRETE PROCESSOR (DP)". It begins at address M.CPC0 with a "START M.CPC0" block. This is followed by an "E-ENABL INHIBIT INTERRUPTS" block, then "READ DIN REGISTER", and "MASK READ WITH DIN INHIBIT WORD". At address DP05C, a decision is made: "ANY TIME PASE DISCRETES". If "YES", it proceeds to "E-ENABL EXECUTE TIME PASE (I) MODULE". If "NO", it bypasses this step. Both paths then reach a decision at address DP08C: "ANY DINs TO BE PROCESSED". If "YES", it goes to "DETERMINE AND PROCESS INDIVIDUAL DINs" at address DP090. If "NO", it bypasses this step. Both paths then reach "RESTORE DIN TABLE HCP CONSTANT" at address DP085. This is followed by "E-ENABL ENABLE INTERRUPTS" and finally "EXIT RETURN" at address DP000.

The flowchart, titled "DISCRETE INPUT 9 (DP9)", outlines the logic for handling guidance failures. It begins with a "START M.DP09" block, followed by a "DISCRETE 9 ENTRY" block. The process then enters a decision point: "GUIDANCE FAILURE". If "YES", it proceeds to "DP195: SET MC27 FOR DP9 AFTER DD4 OR DD4", then "INHIBIT INTERRUPTS", "SET ALL LADDERS TO ZERO", "ENBLE INTERRUPTS", and finally "SET DIN ON MASK TO INHIBIT DIN 9" before "EXIT RETURN". If "NO", it enters another decision point: "IS DIN 9 ON". If "YES", it goes to "DP190: SET DIN ON MASK TO INHIBIT DIN 9", then "SET DIN OFF MASK TO ENAPLE DIN 9", "SET CONTROL FLAG TO CSM ATTITUDE CONTROL", and "EXIT RETURN". If "NO", it goes to "DP185: ALTER DIN OFF MASK TO INHIBIT DIN 9", then "SET DIN ON MASK TO ENABLE DIN 9", and "EXIT RETURN".

The flowchart describes the Digital Command System (DCS) (DS) process. It begins with the M.DS00 module, which starts the system and enables/examines interrupts. The process then reads a discrete input register. A decision is made based on the DCS input word: if it is a data word, the DSAC module (DS559) processes it; if it is a mode word, the DS10 module (DS508) processes it. The DSAC path leads to a decision on DCS data word validity (DS165). If valid, it exits and returns; if not, it issues an error message (DS220). The DS10 path leads to a decision on mode and command word validity (DS45). If valid, it exits and returns; if not, it also leads to the error message (DS220). The error message path leads to a decision on whether termination is required (DS237). If termination is required, it exits and terminates; otherwise, it proceeds to the final exit and return (DS239). Both the direct data path and the error message path lead to the final exit and return (DS239).

If 'NO', it goes to 'DS70', 'IS DATA WORD FORMAT GOOD'. If 'YES', it goes to 'DS90', 'IS DATA SEQUENCE BIT OKAY'. If 'NO', it goes to 'DS80', 'SET ERROR CODE = 44', and 'EXIT DS220'. 'DS90' leads to 'DS130', 'TEST IF MORE WORDS ARE TO BE READ'. If 'YES', it goes to 'DCS COMMAND ROUTINE'. If 'NO', it goes to 'DS140', 'ISSUE CAP FOR DATA WORD', 'OBTAIN SEG. If the time is less than 10 seconds, it issues a Command Response Packet (CRP) (D.S200) and sets an error code (D.S200) to 54, then exits (DS735). Otherwise, it proceeds to read and store input words (DS100) and checks if the mode is active. If active, it issues a CRP (D.S260) and sets the navigation update bit in mode code 27.     ExtracMan --> DS44_80
    DS43_80 -- YES --> ExtracMan
    DS44_80 -- YES --> ExtracMan

The flowchart illustrates the Digital Command System (DCS) (DS) with the following components and logic:

  • START DS22: Initial command.
  • UPDATE SEQUENCE TIME BASE: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S260. If YES, proceed to NAVIGATION UPDATE.
  • NAVIGATION UPDATE: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S330. If YES, proceed to GENERALIZED SWITCH SELECTOR.
  • GENERALIZED SWITCH SELECTOR: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S380. If YES, proceed to MEMORY DUMP REQUEST.
  • MEMORY DUMP REQUEST: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S430. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S430.
  • DS27 > 80: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S430. If YES, proceed to TERMINATE.
  • TERMINATE: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S510. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S510.
  • DS39 > CO: Decision point. If NO, proceed to LADDER MAGNITUDE LIMIT COMMAND. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S510.
  • LADDER MAGNITUDE LIMIT COMMAND: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S900. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S900.
  • DS41 > 80: Decision point. If NO, proceed to EXECUTE GENERALIZED MANEUVER. If YES, proceed to COMPRESSED DATA DUMP.
  • EXECUTE GENERALIZED MANEUVER: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S540. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S540.
  • COMPRESSED DATA DUMP: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S525. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S525.
  • DS33 > 80: Decision point. If NO, proceed to WATER VALVE INHIBIT. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S540.
  • WATER VALVE INHIBIT: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S570. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S570.
  • DS42 > 80: Decision point. If NO, proceed to S-IVB/IU DE-ORBIT COMMAND. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S550.
  • S-IVB/IU DE-ORBIT COMMAND: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S550. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S550.
  • DS43 > 80: Decision point. If NO, proceed to TARGET LOAD. If YES, proceed to EXTRACTION MANEUVER ENABLE COMMAND.
  • TARGET LOAD: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S590. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S590.
  • EXTRACTION MANEUVER ENABLE COMMAND: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S560. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S560.
  • DS38 > 80: Decision point. If NO, proceed to RETURN TO NOMINAL TIMELINE. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S560.
  • RETURN TO NOMINAL TIMELINE: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S560. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S560.
  • DS39 > CO: Decision point. If NO, proceed to SET ERROR CODE IND. MODE COMMAND INVALID. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S560.
  • SET ERROR CODE IND. MODE COMMAND INVALID: Decision point. If NO, exit to EXIT D-S530. If YES, exit to EXIT D-S530.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The memory dump in progress flag must be initialized to zero at start of mission.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: On entry to this module, the starting and ending addresses (including sector and even module) must be given in D.VDLO and D.VDHI respectively, and the memory dump in progress flag, D.FDTL, must be set to minus.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: If a dump is requested when the in progress flag, D.FDTL, is already set, the new request will override the current dump in progress. It is

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: therefore the responsibility of the requesting module to test the in progress flag D.FDTL.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: If a dump is requested in which the starting or ending address is from an odd module, the data from the duplexed even module will be telemetered.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: To terminate a dump in progress, a module must queue-out the Memory Dump Telemetry (M.DT00) and clear the memory dump in progress flag, D.FDTL, to zero.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: During periods of flight in which the F/M computations may be unusually noisy, preset constants are used in place of computed values of D.VFOM. The F/M Calculations module will not be executed after setting D.VFOM to the constant value, as this module will then queue itself out. F.FM will contain the preset constant if it is a non-zero positive value. If the constant is zero, F.FM will be set negative.

The flowchart describes the F/M Calculations (DV) process. It begins at M.DV00 with a 'START' block. The first step is U.F000, which computes the reciprocal of the compensation cycle length. This is followed by DV100, which performs a 'COMP. 2' on the platform measured acceleration. The next step is DV200, which calculates the measured acceleration using equation 4.2.10. A decision point follows: 'SHOULD F/M SET TO A CONSTANT'. If 'YES', it proceeds to DV315, which sets the F/M to a constant. If 'NO', it proceeds to DV210, which computes the M/F smoother. A decision point 'NJ' follows DV210. If 'YES', it proceeds to M.S000, which performs M/F smoothing. If 'NO', it proceeds directly to DV300. The 'RESET F/M CONSTANT FLAG' block is reached from the 'SET F/M TO CONSTANT' block and also from the 'NJ' decision point. Finally, the process moves to DV300, which calculates the telemetek measured acceleration, and ends with an 'EXIT RETURN' block.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: At the end of each computation cycle, the module will mark the end of the current telemetry cycle and the beginning of the next telemetry cycle with an end telemetry cycle (ETC) word followed by a begin telemetry cycle word (BTC). This module will also serve as a telemetry catch-up module; i.e., all telemetry items not telemetered from other modules will be telemetered by the ETC/BTC module. The ETC/BTC module will also reset system status words if necessary.

chunks.label: Text
chunks.content: The Minor Loop Error Monitor module has three basic functions:

chunks.label: List-Group
chunks.content:
1. (1) To monitor the counters of resolver unreasonableness failures to select the resolver to be used by the Minor Loop module.
  2. (2) To monitor the disagreement bit failure counters to control counter selection by the Disagreement Bit Processing module.
  3. (3) To determine if ladder converter A is to be selected by the Minor Loop module.

The flowchart describes the Minor Loop Error Monitor (EC) process. It begins at 'START EC201'. The first decision is 'DISAGREEMENT BIT PROCESSOR ACTIVE'. If 'YES', it proceeds to 'RESET DISAGREEMENT BIT COUNTERS'. If 'NO', it checks 'BOTH COUNTERS BAD'. If 'YES', it triggers 'EC230 B4'. If 'NO', it checks 'GIMBAL ANGLE DISAGREEMENT BIT SET'. If 'YES', it triggers 'SET DG CIRCUITRY FAIL BIT IN MC24'. If 'NO', it proceeds to 'EXCESSIVE A MULTIPLEXER FAILURES'. The 'RESET DISAGREEMENT BIT COUNTERS' step also leads to 'EXCESSIVE A MULTIPLEXER FAILURES'. From 'EXCESSIVE A MULTIPLEXER FAILURES', if 'YES', it triggers 'RESET A MULTIPLEXER FAILURE COUNTER'. If 'NO', it proceeds to 'EXCESSIVE B MULTIPLEXER FAILURES'. The 'RESET A MULTIPLEXER FAILURE COUNTER' step also leads to 'EXCESSIVE B MULTIPLEXER FAILURES'. From 'EXCESSIVE B MULTIPLEXER FAILURES', if 'YES', it leads to 'EXIT EC300'. If 'NO', it triggers 'RESET B MULTIPLEXER FAILURE COUNTER', which then leads to 'EXIT EC300'.

The flowchart, titled "MINOR LOOP ERROR MONITOR (EC)", describes the logic for handling ladder converter errors. It begins at a start point labeled "START EC301". A decision diamond asks "HAS LADDER B CONVERTER BEEN USED?". If the answer is "YES", the process proceeds to "SET LADDER CONVERTER B BITS IN ICR STATUS WORD", which then leads to "SET BIT IN MODE CODE 24 (LAD CONVERTER B PERMANENT)". If the answer is "NO", the process proceeds to "RESET COUNT OF TIMES B LADDER CONVERTOR CHOSEN", which then leads to "(E-ENBL) ENABLE INTERRUPTS". Both paths eventually lead to an "EXIT" point, with the "YES" path labeled "EXIT EC320".
